title: Aerodynamic Optimization of a Multi-Rotor UAV for Power-Line Inspection Using a Coupled CFD-BEMT Framework
content: Predicting the aerodynamic performance of multirotor unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) remains challenging because of complex rotor–rotor and rotor–body interactions. Experimental characterisation of these interactions is often costly and time-consuming, making computational methods valuable for aerodynamic design and optimisation. This study presents a coupled computational ﬂuid dynamics and blade element momentum theory (CFD-BEMT) framework for evaluating a multirotor UAV developed for power-line inspection. The airﬂow was simulated using OpenFOAM, while the propellers were represented as virtual rotors through distributed momentum-source terms calculated using BEMT. The CFD methodology was assessed by comparing predicted Ahmed-body drag coeﬃcients at diﬀerent yaw angles with experimental measurements. Steady-state Reynolds-averaged Navier–Stokes simulations provided satisfactory predictions at low yaw angles, while unsteady simulations generally improved the predictions at higher yaw angles, where large-scale ﬂow separation and wake unsteadiness became signiﬁcant. Standalone static-thrust measurements were also used as reference data to examine changes in rotor loading after integration with the UAV. The computational framework was subsequently applied to a baseline bluﬀ-body conﬁguration, V01, and a redesigned conﬁguration, V02, incorporating smoother fuselage contours, improved payload integration, and modiﬁed rotor placement. A comprehensive simulation matrix was used to investigate the eﬀects of forward velocity, propeller rotational speed, and nose-down angle of attack. The results show that propeller operation substantially modifies the aerodynamic response through nonuniform rotor-induced flow and rotor–body interactions. Compared with V01, the redesigned V02 configuration generally exhibits smaller variations in lift, drag, and lift-to-drag ratio across the investigated angles of attack. However, V02 does not provide uniformly lower drag or a consistently higher lift-to-drag ratio under all operating conditions. Its principal advantage is a more consistent aerodynamic response and reduced sensitivity to changes in nose-down angle of attack. The results demonstrate the capability of the coupled CFD-BEMT framework to assess installation effects, quantify rotor–body interactions, and support the aerodynamic development of multirotor inspection UAVs.
